analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal handgun background checks, gun-lock requirements, and import restrictions on certain firearms.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal federal background checks and gun-safety rules died in committee without a single cosponsor or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Brady Act, which requires licensed gun dealers to run criminal background checks on buyers through the national instant check system. It would also repeal the Child Safety Lock Act, erase the federal 'sporting purposes' tests that restrict import and sale of certain weapons, and strike related gun-storage and safety-device provisions from federal law. It was referred to the House Judiciary and Ways and Means committees and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: People who want to buy firearms without a background check, and firearms manufacturers, importers, and dealers, who would no longer face the Brady Act check requirement, the child safety lock requirement, or the 'sporting purposes' tests that limit which weapons can be imported and sold. Collectors and buyers of currently restricted categories would also gain.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun buyers, dealers, and firearms manufacturers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act of 1993, ending the federal requirement that licensed dealers contact the national instant criminal background check system before transferring a firearm.

Repeals the Child Safety Lock Act of 2005 and related federal provisions on gun storage and gun safety devices, and repeals the section of the 2005 gun-industry liability law that requires secure gun storage or safety devices with handgun transfers.

Strikes the 'sporting purposes' tests from the Internal Revenue Code and the federal criminal code, provisions that currently restrict which firearms and weapons can be imported, sold, or registered based on whether the Attorney General or Secretary finds them suitable for sporting use.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the public would bear the cost in lost screening: purchases by prohibited buyers such as felons and domestic abusers would no longer be checked at the point of sale, and child-safety device requirements would disappear. Law enforcement would lose a tool used to trace gun crimes.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the Brady Act ends the check that stops prohibited purchasers — people with felony convictions, domestic violence records, or other disqualifications — from buying guns through licensed dealers.

Repealing the Child Safety Lock Act and related storage provisions removes federal requirements for secure gun storage and safety devices, which are aimed at preventing child access and accidental shootings.

Eliminating the 'sporting purposes' distinction would remove the legal test used to block import and civilian sale of weapons not considered suitable for recreation, loosening limits on categories of firearms and projectiles currently restricted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real gains to gun buyers and the firearms trade by removing checks, locks, and import tests, but the cost falls on the diffuse public: no point-of-sale screening for prohibited buyers and no safety-device requirements. An honest supporter would have to concede that repealing the Brady Act's background check is a major public-safety change, and the bill as written offered no substitute screening of any kind.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee in early 2007 and sat there with no action, no cosponsors, and no vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Paul introduced the bill on February 15, 2007, and it was referred to the Committee on the Judiciary and, in part, to the Committee on Ways and Means.
On March 19, 2007, the House portion was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, where no further action was taken.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained: the status quo held. Federal background checks, child safety lock requirements, and the sporting-purposes tests all remained in place, and the firearms industry and deregulation supporters got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one — existing gun laws stayed in place

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the record shows no partisan pattern — only a lone Republican sponsor and no committee action under a Democratic majority.

industries.note: The bill would remove the Brady Act check requirement, child safety lock requirements, and the 'sporting purposes' tests that restrict import and sale of certain weapons, widening what they can sell. The gain comes at the cost of public screening for prohibited buyers.

Dealers would no longer have to contact the national instant background check system before every sale, cutting a compliance step and expanding their customer pool to include anyone the check would have stopped.
